entry.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

link.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

entry.content:
For my internship I left my UCLA computational chemistry desk for a while and joined SES AI, a battery company, as an Applied Scientist intern. If you asked me what I worked on, the honest one-line answer is: a lot of things that turned out to be one thing.

The official title I gave the work was multiscale multimodal intelligence across molecules, electrolytes, and cells. That’s a mouthful, so here’s the version I’d tell you over coffee.

The one question

Today’s AI models are very good with pictures and text. They can describe a cat photo and write a poem about it. But chemistry and batteries don’t really live in pictures and text. They live in:

  • 3D geometry: where atoms actually sit in space,
  • physical time: how those atoms jiggle, drift, and react over nanoseconds to months,
  • scales that connect: a tiny change in one molecule showing up, much later, as a battery that lasts longer (or doesn’t).

So the question I kept asking all internship was: can AI understand not just pictures and text, but 3D geometry, physical time, and how the scales connect?

Three scales, one ladder

Think of a battery like a city. The molecules are the people. The electrolyte is the crowd: the liquid the ions swim through, made of salt, solvents, and additives. The cell is the whole city, with its traffic jams, heat waves, and aging infrastructure.

You can’t understand a city from one person’s ID card, and you can’t understand a crowd without watching it move. So the work naturally split into three parts, each climbing one rung of the ladder.

Part 1: molecules (or, “atom is atom, bond is bond”)

People want to search for molecules by drawing them. Papers, unfortunately, draw the same molecule in a dozen outfits: thin double bonds, tiny atom labels, wedges, blurry scans. A human chemist shrugs and says “atom is atom, bond is bond.” A model trained on neat, computer-rendered drawings panics.

I fine-tuned vision-language models to read real paper figures, found that the real bottleneck is the gap between rendered training images and real figures, took a doomed detour through preference optimization, and ended up building a system that would rather say “I’m not sure” than make something up. Then I followed the molecules from 2D drawings all the way into 3D.

👉 Atom is atom, bond is bond

Part 2: electrolytes (or, teaching a puddle to dance)

An electrolyte looks like a boring puddle. Zoom in and it’s a dance floor: lithium ions grabbing solvent partners, anions cutting in, everything shuffling. To simulate that dance you need a rulebook (a force field) and a movie projector (molecular dynamics).

I extended a polarizable force field to new electrolyte molecules, got humbled when a fit that looked perfect on small clusters made the liquid clump, and built a loop that remembers its own failures. Then I taught a model to watch ~40,000 of these movies and learn what a liquid “looks like” from its recipe, a single snapshot, and its motion over time.

👉 Teaching a puddle to dance

Part 3: cells (or, from molecules to batteries)

The question everyone in a battery company actually cares about: if I change the recipe (say, add an additive), what happens to the battery? Does it cycle longer, store better, charge faster?

Real experiments are slow and expensive, so I built a ladder of simulations, from quantum chemistry up to whole-cell heat maps, tried to align all those scales into one shared space, and trained a “world model” that predicts how a cell ages, step by step. The most useful outcomes were honest ones: what connects, what doesn’t, and where the model is too confident.

👉 From molecules to batteries

The thread that ties it together

If there’s one lesson that kept showing up at every scale, it’s this: a pretty number on the training objective is not the same as the scientific goal. A preference model can score beautifully and still get molecules wrong. A force field can nail tiny clusters and still ruin the liquid. An alignment can match molecules perfectly and still say almost nothing about real batteries.

So most of my summer was spent building the checks: agreement between independent readers, liquid simulations as part of the fitting loop, calibration against real measurements. Less glamorous than a leaderboard, but it’s what lets you trust the answer.

Grab a snack. Part 1 starts with a cartoon version of me squinting at a molecule.

entry.title: From molecules to batteries
entry.content:
Part 3 of 3. Previously: Atom is atom, bond is bond and Teaching a puddle to dance. The big picture is in the overview.

We’ve read molecules off paper and watched them dance in a liquid. Now for the question that actually pays the bills at a battery company.

Δrecipe → Δperformance

If I change the recipe, say by adding a pinch of some additive, what changes in the battery? Does it survive more charge cycles? Store better on a shelf? Charge faster? Handle high currents?

It’s a bit like baking. Swap one ingredient and the cake might rise higher, or collapse, or taste fine today and go stale tomorrow. The annoying part is that each real “bake” for a battery is slow and expensive, so real experiments are limited. Compute, on the other hand, is available. The plan: use simulations to fill in the gaps, while real measurements stay the reference. Simulations get to advise; they don’t get to overrule.

A ladder of simulations, in about a month

No single simulation covers everything from electrons to a whole cell heating up, so I built a high-throughput ladder in about a month. Each rung zooms out:

  • DFT: local chemistry and electron transfer. Who gives electrons to whom.
  • MD: the liquid, using the force fields from Part 2.
  • Interface reactions: what happens where the liquid meets the electrode, the battery’s busiest border crossing.
  • kMC (kinetic Monte Carlo): states, events, and rates, like a board game where each move happens with a certain probability per unit time.
  • P2D/SPMe and 3D thermal fields: the whole cell, including temperature and stress.

Can we line up all the scales?

With data from every rung, the natural next idea was to align them, CLIP-style. CLIP is the trick that taught models to put a photo and its caption close together in one shared space. Here, the “photo” and “caption” are a molecule, its liquid, its interface, and its cell. I used a multi-positive InfoNCE loss, which is a fancy way of saying “pull together everything that belongs to the same experiment, push apart everything that doesn’t.”

Two findings, one encouraging and one sobering:

  1. Conditions are essential. Temperature, test protocol, and the like are the glue between scales. When I removed them, the MD-to-electrode link score collapsed from 0.327 to 0.066. Without knowing how a battery was tested, the scales stop recognizing each other.
  2. Molecules ↛ battery just via alignment. Matching a molecule’s identity across views could be strong while the links to real experiments stayed weak. Knowing exactly who someone is doesn’t tell you how they’ll do at their new job.

A world model for aging

Batteries are a story told over time: they age, cycle by cycle. So instead of predicting the ending directly, I trained a world model: learn from aging simulations to predict the next state, then roll it out, feeding each prediction back in as the next input. Like predicting tomorrow’s weather, then using that forecast to predict the day after.

That’s a harsh test, because small errors snowball. So I checked four things: next-step accuracy, long-run drift, whether it gets the direction of change right, and calibration to real experiments.

  • I compared 41 architectures. The learned world model beat a direct MLP baseline on simulated sequences.
  • That does not by itself prove transfer to real cells. Simulated sequences are the practice field, not the match.
  • Calibration to experiments supported 24 targets.
  • The uncertainty was overconfident: nominal 90% intervals actually covered about 68–78%. When the model said “I’m 90% sure,” it should have said “eh, maybe 70%.” Good to know, and now it’s written down.

The VC mystery

My favorite moment came from one additive, VC. Its trends differed between two different cell designs: same ingredient, different story depending on the cell. The physics model reproduced some of the direction changes, but not the full size of the effect.

That sounds like a failure, but it’s actually the most useful kind of result. “The model gets the direction but not the magnitude” points at a specific missing mechanism, and that became the next mechanism test. A good model doesn’t just answer questions; it tells you which experiment to run next.

A cell co-scientist

As with the electrolytes, I wrapped the pieces into a co-scientist: an LLM that pulls in multi-scale evidence and calls tools, with chemistry-aware tokenization so chemical names get read as chemistry, not random letter soup. The interface shows every tool call and record ID, and it keeps measured, computed, and predicted values clearly separated. If you’ve read this far, you know why that last part matters to me.

Wrapping up the summer

Across molecules, electrolytes, and cells, the same pattern kept repeating: the exciting number is rarely the whole truth, and the honest checks are where the real progress hides. Agreement over confidence. Liquid tests over cluster fits. Calibration over leaderboards.

Thanks for reading all three parts. If you want the map again, it lives in the overview. Now if you’ll excuse me, I have a mechanism test to think about.

entry.title: Teaching a puddle to dance
entry.content:
Part 2 of 3. Previously: Atom is atom, bond is bond. The big picture is in the overview.

In Part 1 the molecules were sitting still for their portraits. Now we drop them into a liquid and ask a much harder question from my slides: how do molecules move in their micro-environment?

Meet the puddle

An electrolyte is the liquid inside a battery that ions swim through. The recipe is simple: salt + solvents + additives. The behavior is not. Zoom in and it’s a crowded dance floor: lithium ions grab solvent molecules as partners, anions try to cut in, and how fast everyone moves across the floor decides how well the battery charges and discharges.

The rulebook and the movie

Two words you need for this post:

  • A force field is the rulebook for how atoms push and pull on each other.
  • Molecular dynamics (MD) is playing the movie with that rulebook: you put lots of molecules in a box, apply the rules, and watch.

If the rulebook is wrong, the movie is fiction. And the existing rulebook didn’t cover some of the new electrolyte molecules we cared about. So my first job was to extend a polarizable force field (one where the electron clouds can squish in response to their neighbors, which matters a lot around small, charged ions like lithium).

The recipe:

  1. Compute quantum (DFT) reference data on small lithium and sodium clusters. Some are binary (the ion with one partner); some are ternary (solvent and anion competing for the same lithium, like two people reaching for the last slice of pizza).
  2. Fit mainly the exp-6 term, the part of the rulebook covering short-range repulsion (“personal space!”) and dispersion (the weak, sticky attraction between everything).
  3. Test in liquid MD: density, radial distribution functions (who stands next to whom), diffusion, and conductivity.

The fit that looked perfect

Here’s the plot twist. One fit looked great on the clusters. Errors low, curves lined up, very satisfying.

Then I ran the liquid. It clumped. The ions huddled together in big clusters like penguins in a blizzard, and transport ended up far from what’s measured experimentally.

I traced it back to an ether-oxygen interaction that the fit had effectively broken. Restoring it brought the cluster fraction down from about 0.81 to 0.28, and conductivity moved closer to measurement.

The lesson, which I now believe in my bones: MD validation is part of parameter development, not a final demo. Small clusters can’t tell you everything about a liquid. You have to watch the movie.

A loop that remembers its mistakes

So I built that into a loop, which I called RSI:

The key part is step three. Every failure gets saved as searchable memory: the conditions, the bad parameters, the symptoms, and the checks that caught it. The next time a fit starts drifting toward “penguin huddle,” there’s a record that says we’ve seen this before, here’s what it looked like.

Honest caveat: a proper fixed-budget test of whether this memory actually makes research faster is still on my to-do list. It feels faster. Feelings aren’t data.

40,000 movies

Once you can make movies, you can make a lot of them. We had about 40,000 MD trajectories × 5,000 frames each, roughly 200 million frames. Way more than any human could watch. So I asked: can a model learn what a liquid “is” from watching?

I looked at the same liquid through three views:

  • the recipe (what went into the bottle),
  • a snapshot (one frozen frame of atoms in 3D),
  • the trajectory (how things move over time).

The snapshot encoder treats each frame as a periodic graph (atoms connected to neighbors within 6 Å), and passes messages with an equivariant network, one that tracks both plain numbers and directions, so rotating the box doesn’t confuse it. Each frame becomes 128 learned + 8 geometric numbers.

The unglamorous engineering

200 million frames is a lot of frames. Two things made it tractable:

  • Neighbor search went from O(N²) to O(N): instead of every atom asking every other atom “are you close?”, each atom only checks its own neighborhood.
  • I froze the snapshot encoder and cached every frame once. The cache is about 52 GB and cost about 395 GPU-hours, one time. After that, a training step went from 12.6 s to 0.15 s.

That’s the difference between “let’s try an idea” and “let’s try an idea next week.”

What the model learned

  • Retrieval@10 (can you find the matching liquid in the top 10?) was 84.1% with the full representation versus 82.4% from static structure alone. Surprise: a single snapshot already knows a lot!
  • Conductivity R² of 0.976, close to a strong descriptor baseline.
  • Adding trajectory features improved conductivity error in 18 of 21 held-out chemistry groups. Motion helps, especially on chemistry the model hasn’t seen.

I also played with generating trajectories (rolling the movie forward with GRU, TCN, and causal-transformer models), which was fun and is a story for another day.

An electrolyte scientist sidekick

Finally, I wrapped the tools into an “electrolyte scientist” assistant: an LLM planner with a harness and a registry of tools (reading files, checking protocols, running analysis programs, keeping evidence records). You can ask it why a simulation failed, how a formulation performed, or how to prepare a run at a new temperature. The researcher stays in the loop and reviews what it proposes to try next. Sidekick, not replacement.

Next stop: the whole battery

Molecules and liquids are fun, but nobody buys a puddle. In Part 3, we try to connect all of this to actual batteries, and find out where the connections hold and where they snap: From molecules to batteries.
entry.summary: Part 2 of my SES AI internship: force fields, liquids that clump, and learning from 40,000 molecular movies

entry.title: Atom is atom, bond is bond

link.title: Atom is atom, bond is bond

entry.content:
Part 1 of 3. Start with the overview if you haven’t.

Here’s a scene from my slides. A cartoon scientist (me, basically) looks at a drawing of a molecule.

Me: Who are you?

Molecule: NaPF6 in FEC.

Lovely. Polite molecule. Now I show it a second drawing of the same thing, in a different style.

Molecule: Same here.

Model: Hmm…

Me: Haha, the same.

Same molecule, many outfits

People want to search chemistry by drawing: sketch a structure, find every paper that mentions it. The catch is that papers draw the same molecule in wildly different styles. Thin double bonds. Atom labels the size of a dust mite. Wedge bonds. Scans that look like they went through a fax machine twice.

A chemist looks at all of these and says the thing that became my motto for the summer: “Atom is atom, bond is bond.” The style doesn’t matter. The model, at first, disagreed.

The real bottleneck

The obvious fix is “train on more drawings.” And it’s easy to generate endless drawings with chemistry software, so you can produce a model that looks amazing. (My slides had a joke here: “99.5% accuracy (reported by me).”)

But the real bottleneck wasn’t the amount of data. It was distribution shift: the gap between tidy, computer-rendered training images and messy, real paper figures. A model that aces the rendered exam can still flunk the real world.

So I went and got real data: about 38K molecule crops from papers. Since nobody hands you ground-truth labels for those, I ran four independent readers and kept a label only when 3 of 4 agreed.

Teaching the model

Model: Teach me.

I fine-tuned vision-language models (supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, a lightweight way to adapt a big model without retraining all of it). I compared 3 base models and 6 mixtures of real and synthetic images. To keep myself honest, I split the data by molecule identity and removed 55,267 benchmark molecules (by InChIKey, a chemical fingerprint) from training, so the model couldn’t just memorize the test.

The winner: GLM trained with 70% real images, reaching 59.8% exact structure on 331 figures from ACS journals, statistically comparable to MolScribe (58.3%), a strong established reader. I wrote more about the real-vs-synthetic story in an earlier note.

The DPO detour

Then I got ambitious and tried DPO, a preference-tuning method that teaches a model to prefer good answers over bad ones. The training curves were gorgeous: loss dropped from 0.69 to 0.19, preference accuracy hit 90–97%.

Exact match on the molecules it actually generated? 0–2%.

The model had learned to win the preference game, not to read molecules. A second attempt improved validity but still landed at roughly half the accuracy of plain fine-tuning. So I kept SFT and walked away with the lesson I now repeat to anyone who’ll listen: a pretty training score can miss the scientific goal.

VERDICT: allowed to say “I don’t know”

Back to the comic:

Me: You got it, go label more real molecule depictions in papers.

Model: Yes, ma’am, even though I have high confidence, there is no ground truth. Is it reliable?

Great question, model. That’s what VERDICT answers.

Instead of trusting one model, VERDICT asks my fine-tuned VLM plus three open-source readers. It compares their answers by chemical identity (InChIKey), not raw strings, because two different strings can describe the same molecule. It keeps the disagreements and the sources, and it’s allowed to abstain.

The nice part: whether the readers agree turns out to be a great signal for whether the answer is right. Agreement separates right from wrong answers with an AUROC of about 0.916, compared with 0.547 for checking how similar a redrawn image looks to the original (which is barely better than a coin flip). Retraining on what the loop collected gave mixed gains, so I report data quality and model improvement separately rather than blending them into one happy number.

From flat drawings to 3D

Reading the drawing is just step one. The full pipeline goes: 2D image → SMILES → 3D conformer → energies and forces (with machine-learned potentials like MACE and UMA).

Why bother with 3D? A molecule has several “views.” SMILES is a line of text. A graph says who’s bonded to whom. A 3D structure says where everything actually sits in space. It’s like describing a friend by their name, their family tree, or their photo.

I tested 2D alone, 3D alone, 2D+3D, and a sneaky control: 2D plus shuffled 3D, to check whether the model was really using the geometry or just enjoying extra numbers. In the controlled test, adding real 3D cut energy error by about 18.2% and volume error by about 49.4%. Geometry matters.

Two more humbling findings:

  • Cross-view retrieval ≠ property prediction. Being good at matching a molecule’s SMILES to its 3D shape doesn’t mean you’re good at predicting what it does.
  • I trained a SMILES “student” to copy a 3D “teacher.” It matched the teacher’s vectors nicely, and gave no gain on conductivity. Copying the homework isn’t the same as understanding it.

What I took away

Real data beats more synthetic data. Agreement is a better trust signal than confidence. And 3D helps, but only if you check that it helps the thing you care about.

Molecules don’t live alone, though. Next, they jump into a liquid and start dancing: Teaching a puddle to dance.
entry.summary: Part 1 of my SES AI internship: teaching models to read molecules from real papers, and then to see them in 3D

entry.title: Real data, not more synthetic data, closes the OCSR gap

link.title: Real data, not more synthetic data, closes the OCSR gap

entry.content:
A short summary of what we found in Real Data Closes Synthetic-to-Real Gap in Optical Chemical Structure Recognition.

Optical chemical structure recognition looks solved if you only test on rendered molecules. The starting recognizer, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, reaches over 91% accuracy on synthetic images — and below 16% on the ACS, CLEF-IP and USPTO benchmarks, which are real document crops. That gap is the whole problem: millions of structures exist only as drawings inside patents and papers.

So we fine-tuned 21 recognizers on mixtures of synthetically rendered structures and labeled real depictions from patents, journal figures and hand-drawn collections, varying three things independently: the base VLM, the fraction of real training data, and whether the vision tower was adapted.

Real data is the variable that matters

For Qwen2.5-VL, ACS exact match goes from 0.15 with no real data, to 0.37 at 9.5% real data, to 0.46 at 50.2%. A tenth of the training mixture being real is worth more than anything else we varied — which is a useful thing to know when labeling real depictions is the expensive part.

Vision-tower LoRA is base-dependent

Adapting the vision tower is usually treated as a knob you turn on. It isn’t:

  • Qwen2.5-VL: +0.00, paired p = 1.00 — no effect at all.
  • InternVL3-8B: +22.8 to +34.6 points.
  • GLM-4.1V-9B: a modest gain.

Same task, same data, opposite conclusions depending on the backbone. Any claim of the form “vision LoRA helps VLM fine-tuning” needs the base model attached to it.

Choose the base and the mixture together

The spread between base models is largest with no real data (0.21) and shrinks to 0.06 at 70% real data — and the ranking changes along the way. Picking a backbone on a synthetic-only ablation and then scaling up real data can leave you on the wrong model.

The strongest recognizer ends at 0.96 exact match on clean renders and 0.49, 0.65, 0.84 and 0.76 on ACS, CLEF-IP, UOB and USPTO respectively. Real documents are still far from solved — which is why the production path we ship, VERDICT, is an ensemble that abstains rather than a single model that always answers.
entry.summary: What 21 fine-tuned recognizers say about mixing synthetic and real training images
